videos.title: What would happen if you dug a hole straight through the Earth and then jumped in?
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
What would happen if you dug a hole straight through the Earth and then jumped in?
Would you get stuck in the middle?
Would you bounce back and forth forever?
Would you go accelerating out the other side?
So what happens is you jump in and you start accelerating down towards the center due to the force of gravity from all of the Earth beneath you.
You're falling faster and faster and faster, but as you get towards the center, there's less mass pulling you down.
So when you reach the center after about 21 minutes, the Earth is going to be pulling you equally in all directions.
Now, if you teleported in there, you'd be stuck forever.
But lucky for you, in this scenario, you're traveling over 11 km per second or 25,000 miles an hour.
So you're just going straight on through and you'd slow down as you reach the other side, finally coming to a stop.
Unless someone catches you there, you're going right on back.
So you're bouncing back and forth basically forever.
In real life, the deepest anyone has ever dug is a third of the way through the crust in the 1970s and we're making a longer video all about it, so subscribe.
videos.caption:
What if I dug a hole through the Earth and jumped in?

Would I get stuck in the middle? Would I bounce from side to side?

In real life, the deepest anyone has ever dug is .2% of the way to the center. And yet, we know a surprising amount about what’s down below our feet...

videos.title: What would happen if you drilled a hole straight through the ice in Antarctica and jumped in?
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
What would happen if you drilled a hole straight through the ice in Antarctica and jumped in?
There's something crazy down there.
So what happens is you jump in and the snow around you quickly changes to dense blue ice.
As you go deeper, you realize the air bubbles trapped all around you are from the time of the Renaissance on the surface, then ancient Rome, then the last Ice Age, but the pressure keeps rising, and you keep getting closer to Earth's hot core.
So 4 km down, the ice suddenly turns to water.
You're inside a lake.
A massive lake, trapped completely under the surface, sealed off from the rest of the world for at least 15 million years.
So, inside that lake, you might see life forms that have been evolving in total isolation.
We know it's there because scientists bounced the radio waves through the ice and spotted this smooth, flat line, meaning liquid water.
And in 2012, a Russian team finally reached it with a special drill, but right as the water was going to rush into the borehole, they stopped and they let a tiny bit of lake water freeze in that hole and brought the ice up for study.
And they found some unusual bacterial DNA, but nothing conclusive yet about more complex animals.
Scientists want to go back, but it's controversial.
They worry about contamination, but we now know that there are over 400 lakes down there, and something else, if you want to know what, follow for more.
videos.caption:
What would happen if you drilled a hole straight through the ice in Antarctica and jumped in?

You jump in and the snow around you quickly changes to dense blue ice. As you go deeper, you realize the air bubbles trapped all around you are from the time of the Renaissance on the surface, then Ancient Rome, then the last Ice Age!

But the pressure is rising and you’re getting closer to Earth’s hot core, the ice suddenly turns into…

To find out what it is, follow along!

videos.title: If you've ever thought, what if I just dug a really, really deep hole?
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
If you've ever thought, what if I just dug a really, really deep hole?
That's what the USSR did right here.
That hole is 12.2 km or 7.6 mi deep.
That makes it deeper than the Mariana Trench.
It's deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
The USSR dug it starting in 1970.
It was part of a race to see who could retrieve a sample from the Earth's mantle first, kind of a space race, but the opposite.
The United States only reached 600 ft before pulling funding, but the USSR kept going for 20 years.
They made it about a third of the way through Earth's crust before the temperature got a lot hotter than they expected.
Their drill bits started melting.
The rock was so hot, it was like plastic, but along the way, they invented all kinds of drilling and scientific equipment that we still use today.
They found fossils of organisms dating back 2 billion years and discovered that there was water much deeper than previously thought.
It's crazy though that the deepest hole humanity has ever dug is still .002% of the way to the middle of the Earth.
There is so much that we still don't know about our own planet.
If you like optimistic science and tech stories, follow for more.
videos.caption:
What if you just… keep digging? That’s what the USSR did in 1970. This hole is 7.6 miles or 12.2 kilometers deep, making it deeper than the deepest part of the ocean and deeper than Mt. Everest is tall.

It was part of a race to see who could retrieve a sample from Earth’s mantle first - kind of like the space race, but DOWN. Here’s what they found... 

Humanity’s deepest hole is only 0.2% of the way to the middle of the Earth. There’s still so much left to learn about our own planet.

videos.title: This is a drawing of a normal modern animal that you'd recognize.
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
This is a drawing of a normal modern animal that you'd recognize.
Except they drew it in a way that many early science illustrators drew dinosaurs, with the skin just wrapped around the bone without muscle, turning this normal animal into a monster.
Can you guess what it is?
That's a zebra.
Okay, what about this one?
That's a baboon.
This one's my favorite, can you guess this one?
That's a hippo.
This practice is called shrink-wrapping, and it caused a lot of really big misunderstandings about what dinosaurs actually looked like.
They were way chunkier than people think.
Artists and scientists are correcting that now, they're adding more loose skin and muscles and fatty tissues.
They're showing dinosaurs like the animals they really were.
If you want to see what dinosaurs really look like, we made a longer video.
And follow for optimistic science and tech stories.
videos.caption:
Can you guess this animal?

This is a drawing of a modern animal by @cmkosemen - showing what it would look like if you drew it the way many early science illustrators drew dinosaurs. Those illustrators just drew skin wrapped around bone without muscle, turning this normal animal into a monster.

This is called “shrink wrapping” and it has affected the way a lot of us think about what dinosaurs looked like…

If you want to know more about dinosaurs, watch our longer video!  And subscribe for optimistic science and tech stories…

videos.title: Have you ever wondered what if you just kept going away from Earth?
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
Have you ever wondered what if you just kept going away from Earth?
Imagine you fly off at the speed of light.
At 8.3 minutes, you'd reach our sun.
After 4 hours and 6 minutes, you'd pass the farthest planet in our solar system, and you'd have to get through this mess of comets and asteroids.
How long do you think it takes you at the speed of light to get to the farthest object humans have ever sent?
It's 23 hours and 19 minutes.
Now, way beyond that, at 29 days, you'd hit this cloud of icy debris.
Even traveling at the speed of light, it takes a year and a half to go through it.
But hold on, at 4 years in, just as you're passing our nearest star, something weird happens.
You notice that you're in kind of a clearing.
It turns out that our solar system is inside this local bubble.
At about 100 years, you pass where the edge of our radio bubble is now, the distance our radio waves have traveled out into the universe.
Compared to our whole galaxy, that distance is just that tiny blue spot.
It would take you 27,000 years to reach the center and another 50,000 years to reach the other edge.
And if you kept going and going and going for 46.5 billion years, you'd reach the edge of our observable universe, and beyond that, the light from whatever is out here still hasn't had time to reach Earth in the whole history of the universe.
So, maybe you'd find out.
If you like this video, subscribe.
videos.caption:
What if you just keep going?

Imagine you fly off at the speed of light. After 8.3 minutes, you’d reach our Sun. After 4 hours and 6 minutes, you’d pass the furthest planet in our solar system.

How long do you think it takes you at the speed of light to get to the farthest object humans have ever sent? Follow if you think less than 24 hours.

But at 4 years in, just as you’re passing our nearest star… something weird happens…

videos.title: This is the first ever footage of a giant squid in its natural habitat.
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
This is the first ever footage of a giant squid in its natural habitat.
It took decades and a lot of creative engineering.
Step one: remove all the sound.
Scientists removed all the motors off of their camera and they let it just float in place.
Step two: remove all the lights.
But that's really hard when you want to get footage.
They need some form of light.
So scientists looked at other deep sea creatures like this vampire squid and they noticed they're not black, but red.
Red wavelengths are very long and they're quickly swallowed up by water.
It's why the ocean appears blue.
So scientists put red LED lights on the camera, making that light invisible to the animals down here.
But you need something familiar to lure in a sea monster, like a bright, blue lure.
And it worked.
Within hours, a giant squid appeared out of nowhere gripping onto the device.
It was the first time we had ever seen an adult giant squid in its natural habitat, but now there's another way to find animals in the deep sea.
To see it, you got to follow along.
videos.caption:
How they found the giant squid…

This is the first ever footage of a giant squid in its natural habitat. It took decades to get this footage. And some creative engineering.

The further down into the ocean you go the darker it gets, so when scientists make their way down there with ROV’s or subs the lights and motors typically cause animals adapted for cold, dark isolation to flee. 

In 2012, one scientist got creative and finally caught some incredible footage of a deep sea creature we’d never seen before in its natural habitat. For more, subscribe!  

#deepsea #seamonster #ocean #science

videos.title: Roughly a million people are attending the 2024 US Open in New York, but roughly 15 million fans like me...
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
Roughly a million people are attending the 2024 US Open in New York, but roughly 15 million fans like me follow the tournament on the US Open app and their website, and there is a lot of action to follow, two weeks, 22 courts, hundreds of matches, so to make it easier to keep up, IBM and the United States Tennis Association, partnered to create this, it's a match report, and they make them for every single match, hundreds of them, they do it with AI, specifically IBM's Watson X.
First they trained foundation models like IBM Granet to understand the language of the US Open so they can translate the roughly 10,000 data points from each match into written summaries, and what's even cooler is that IBM publishes the data sources that were used to train Granet, which is really important, good AI starts with good data, and once the models are trained, they can also use them to create AI commentary or likelihood to win, so the USDA editorial team can produce more of the content that tennis fans love, if you want to learn more about it go to ibm.com/usopen.

videos.title: This incredible new LEGO smart brick is full of new tech and it's going to bring my Lego set to life in a...
videos.creator: Cleo Abram
videos.transcript:
This incredible new LEGO smart brick is full of new tech and it's going to bring my Lego set to life in a totally new way.
This is the biggest innovation in Lego bricks in my lifetime, and I love LEGO sets.
So, here we go.
So first, you build the new LEGO Star Wars Smart play sets just like we all know and love.
And then, to play with it, you add the special smart brick, smart tag, and smart minifigures, which means for the first time ever, the Lego Star Wars Galaxy will come alive.
Inside the smart brick, there's a gyroscope sensor that knows its orientation so that when I do this, it's got a distance sensor to know how far from the smart minifigures it is.
So that when I do this, and it's even got a color sensor to know what it's next to.
This feels like even more of what I've always loved about Lego sets.
How they spark your imagination, how they immerse you in stories without screens, and you can play again and again.
Now, I really want to build this one, but I'm saving it to give to the kids in my life that I love.
If you want one for a kid that you love or for yourself, check out Lego Smart Play.
videos.caption: The new LEGO SMART Play sets are full of tech that bring my LEGO sets...to life. Here’s how. @lego #LEGOPartner #LEGOSMARTPlay #LEGOStarWars #LEGOUnboxing #LEGO2026
